meta.session_title: Day 1 - Introduction to Java & Language Fundamentals

overview.summary: This session introduces the Java platform architecture (JVM/JDK/JRE), all 8 primitive data types, operators, flow control structures, and arrays. Every concept is grounded in both academic understanding and real-world banking/finance use cases so you can immediately apply what you learn.
learning_outcomes: Explain the difference between JVM, JRE, and JDK and why Java is platform-independent
Declare and use all 8 Java primitive types with appropriate sizes and ranges
Apply arithmetic, relational, logical, and bitwise operators correctly
Implement flow control: if/else, switch, for, while, do-while, break, continue
Create, populate, and traverse 1D arrays and use the Arrays utility class
Apply Java naming conventions and basic best practices
prerequisite_knowledge: Basic understanding of what a computer program is
Familiarity with any one programming language (optional but helpful)

sections.title: Java Platform: JVM, JRE, JDK

images.caption: JDK → JRE → JVM containment hierarchy and roles
images.alt: Diagram showing JDK containing JRE containing JVM, with labels for development tools, standard libraries, and bytecode executor
images.note: Replace with custom diagram if preferred

images.caption: Java Write Once Run Anywhere — same .class file on Windows, Linux, macOS
images.alt: Diagram showing .java source compiled to .class bytecode, then running on Windows JVM, Linux JVM, and macOS JVM
images.note: Replace with custom WORA diagram if preferred

sections.content:
Java's power comes from its platform independence. When you write a Java program, it is compiled not into machine-specific binary code, but into bytecode — a set of instructions for the Java Virtual Machine (JVM). This bytecode is stored in .class files. The JVM on each operating system knows how to interpret this bytecode and execute it natively. This is why Java's slogan is 'Write Once, Run Anywhere' (WORA).

The three layers of the Java platform are:

1. JVM (Java Virtual Machine): The engine that executes bytecode. It is platform-specific — there is a JVM for Windows, Linux, macOS, etc. The JVM performs memory management, garbage collection, and JIT (Just-In-Time) compilation to speed up execution.

2. JRE (Java Runtime Environment): The JVM plus the standard Java class libraries (java.lang, java.util, java.io, etc.). If you only want to RUN Java programs, install the JRE.

3. JDK (Java Development Kit): The JRE plus development tools — javac (compiler), javadoc (documentation generator), jar (archive tool), jdb (debugger). Developers must install the JDK.

Memory aid: JDK ⊃ JRE ⊃ JVM — each layer contains the one inside it.

In banking applications, Java's platform independence means a core banking system built in Java can run on Linux servers in the data center, Windows developer laptops, and even Android ATM interfaces — using the same codebase.

sections.title: Primitive Data Types

images.caption: Java 8 Primitive Data Types — sizes, ranges, and default values
images.alt: Table showing all 8 Java primitive types with size in bytes, default value, and value range
images.note: Replace with cleaner custom table image if preferred

sections.content:
Java has 8 primitive data types — the building blocks for all values in your programs. Unlike objects, primitives are stored directly on the stack for fast access.

Choosing the right type matters in production systems. In banking:
- Use 'long' for account numbers (can be very large)
- Use 'double' for display, but BigDecimal for ACTUAL monetary calculations (precision required!)
- Use 'byte' or 'short' for status codes (saves memory when millions of records exist)
- Use 'boolean' for flags: isActive, isFrozen, hasOverdraft
- Use 'char' for single-character codes: transaction type ('D' for debit, 'C' for credit)

key_points: Integer literals over int range need 'L' suffix (long); float literals need 'f' suffix
Underscores in numeric literals (1_00_000) improve readability — valid from Java 7+
For financial calculations, always use java.math.BigDecimal, NOT double (floating-point precision errors)
common_mistakes: Using int for account numbers > 2.1 billion — silent overflow, no exception!
Using double for money calculations: 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004 in floating-point

sections.title: Operators

images.caption: Java Operator Precedence Table
images.alt: Java operator precedence table from highest (unary) to lowest (assignment), showing all operator categories
images.note: Replace with custom precedence chart if preferred

sections.content:
Java operators allow you to perform computations, comparisons, and logical decisions. Understanding operator precedence prevents subtle bugs.

Arithmetic operators: +, -, *, /, % (modulo/remainder)
- Integer division truncates: 7 / 2 = 3 (not 3.5)
- Modulo is powerful: n % 2 == 0 checks even/odd; it's also used for cyclic patterns

Relational operators: ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= — return boolean
Logical operators: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT) — with short-circuit evaluation
Assignment operators: =, +=, -=, *=, /=, %=
Increment/Decrement: ++ and -- (pre and post forms)
Ternary: condition ? trueValue : falseValue — compact if-else
Bitwise: &, |, ^, ~, <<, >> — used in flags and performance-critical code

examples.title: Interest Calculation using Operators
examples.description: Compute Simple and Compound Interest for a loan scenario
examples.output:
Simple Interest: ₹135000.00
Compound Interest: ₹145680.85
Difference (Compound vs Simple): ₹10680.85
Loan Category: HOME_SMALL

key_points: Short-circuit evaluation: in (a && b), if 'a' is false, 'b' is never evaluated — use this to prevent NullPointerException
Integer division always truncates toward zero: -7/2 = -3 (not -4)
% operator returns same sign as dividend: -7%3 = -1 in Java
common_mistakes: Using == to compare String objects (compares references, not content — use .equals())
Forgetting that x++ returns the OLD value while ++x returns the NEW value

sections.title: Flow Control

images.caption: Java Flow Control — if/else, switch, for, while, do-while decision diagram
images.alt: Flowchart showing Java flow control structures: if-else branching and loop flowcharts
images.note: Replace with custom ATM flow diagram for banking context

images.caption: while vs do-while — execution order difference
images.alt: Side-by-side flowchart comparing while loop (condition before body) and do-while loop (body before condition)

sections.content:
Flow control structures let your program make decisions and repeat actions. They are the backbone of business logic — from validating a PIN to processing thousands of transactions.

Decision structures:
- if / else if / else: evaluate conditions and branch
- switch: efficient multi-way branch on int, char, String, or enum values (Java 14+ has switch expressions)

Looping structures:
- for: use when you know the iteration count
- while: use when the iteration count is unknown, check condition first
- do-while: always executes at least once, check condition after (useful for menus)
- enhanced for (for-each): clean iteration over arrays and collections

Loop control:
- break: exits the loop entirely
- continue: skips current iteration, moves to next

examples.description: Simulate ATM withdrawal with balance check, PIN validation, and transaction loop
examples.output:
PIN correct. Welcome!
Dispensed ₹5000. Remaining balance: ₹20000.00
Insufficient funds. Balance: ₹20000.00
Dispensed ₹1000. Remaining balance: ₹19000.00

key_points: switch on String is allowed since Java 7; switch on int, char, byte, short always allowed
do-while guarantees at least one execution — ideal for menu loops and PIN retry logic
break in a for-each loop works the same as in a traditional for loop
common_mistakes: Forgetting 'break' in switch cases causes fall-through to the next case
Infinite loop: while(true) without a guaranteed break condition

sections.title: Arrays

images.caption: Java Array Memory Layout — indices 0 to length-1 in contiguous memory
images.alt: Diagram showing a Java array with indexed boxes, showing element at index 0 (first) through length-1 (last), stored contiguously in heap memory
images.note: Replace with custom array visualization showing banking context (e.g., transaction amounts)

sections.content:
An array is a fixed-size, ordered collection of elements of the same type. Arrays are zero-indexed — the first element is at index 0. Arrays are objects in Java (stored in the heap), even though their element types can be primitives.

Key characteristics:
- Fixed size once created (unlike ArrayList, which is dynamic)
- Elements accessed by index: arr[0], arr[1], ..., arr[n-1]
- Length property: arr.length (no parentheses — it's a field, not a method)
- Default values: int[] defaults to 0, double[] to 0.0, boolean[] to false, Object[] to null

The java.util.Arrays class provides powerful utility methods: sort(), binarySearch(), copyOf(), fill(), equals(), toString().

In banking, arrays model: transaction history (fixed window), branch list, EMI installments, exchange rates for a day.

key_points: arr.length is a field (no parentheses); String.length() is a method (with parentheses)
Arrays.sort() modifies in place; use Arrays.copyOf() if you need the original
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is a runtime exception — always validate index bounds
common_mistakes: Accessing arr[arr.length] — the valid range is 0 to arr.length-1
Comparing arrays with == (compares references); use Arrays.equals(a, b) for content comparison

sections.title: Best Practices & Java Coding Standards
sections.content:
Professional Java code follows naming conventions and coding standards that make it readable, maintainable, and reviewable. These are not enforced by the compiler but are enforced by code reviewers in any reputable company.

Naming conventions:
- Classes/Interfaces: PascalCase — BankAccount, LoanCalculator, Serializable
- Methods/Variables: camelCase — calculateEMI(), accountBalance, isActive
- Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE — MAX_WITHDRAWAL_LIMIT, DEFAULT_INTEREST_RATE
- Packages: all lowercase — com.robobank.core, com.robobank.service
- Booleans: use is/has/can/should prefix — isEligible(), hasOverdraft()

Code quality:
- One statement per line
- Meaningful names: 'interestRate' not 'ir', 'accountBalance' not 'ab'
- Avoid magic numbers: use named constants (final int MAX_PIN_ATTEMPTS = 3)
- Comment the 'why', not the 'what' — code shows what; comment explains business rule

syntax_box.description: Constants and naming in a banking class

key_points: Naming conventions are team contracts — inconsistency breaks code readability at scale
Magic numbers make code unreadable: 'if (attempts == 3)' vs 'if (attempts == MAX_PIN_ATTEMPTS)'
final keyword on a variable makes it a constant — the value cannot change after assignment
common_mistakes: Using single-letter variable names (except i, j, k for loop counters by convention)
Putting multiple statements on one line — makes debugging very hard

home_assignment.title: Day 1 Home Assignment: Java Fundamentals + Banking Domain
home_assignment.description: Write a Java program that models a simple bank account. The program should: (1) Declare variables using all 8 primitive types for account data, (2) Compute simple and compound interest using operators, (3) Use if/else and switch for account type and transaction type logic, (4) Store and analyze a transaction history array (5 transactions), (5) Print a summary using a for loop. Push to GitHub with a README.
hints: Use 'long' for account number (it can exceed int range)
Use 'char' for account type ('S', 'C') and transaction type ('D', 'C', 'T')
Use Arrays.sort() and a loop to find max/min transaction
Name your constants with UPPER_SNAKE_CASE: MIN_BALANCE, MAX_WITHDRAWAL
